Healthcare Leadership Council • 750 9th Street, NW Suite 500, Washington, DC 20001 • www.hlc.org 
 
June 15, 2026 
 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS-0062-P 
Mail Stop: C4-26-05 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
 
RE: Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P) 
Dear Administrator Oz:  
The Healthcare Leadership Council (HLC) and the Confidentiality Coalition (collectively, HLC and the 
Coalition) appreciate the opportunity to comment on Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient 
Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for 
Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, 
Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and 
Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges Proposed Rule (CMS-
0062-P).1 The proposed rule aims to improve the electronic exchange of healthcare data and 
streamline processes related to prior authorization, goals that we strongly support.  
HLC is an association of CEOs and C-suite executives from all sectors of healthcare working to 
shape the future of the U.S. healthcare system. HLC is the exclusive forum for the nation’s 
healthcare industry leaders to lead on major, sector-wide issues, generate innovative solutions to 
unleash private sector ingenuity, and advocate for policies to improve our nation’s healthcare 
delivery system. Members of HLC – hospitals, academic health centers, health plans, 
pharmaceutical companies, medical device manufacturers, laboratories, biotech firms, health 
product distributors/ wholesalers, post-acute care providers, homecare providers, group purchasing 
organizations, and information technology companies – advocate for measures to increase the 
quality and efficiency of healthcare through a patient-centered approach. 
The Confidentiality Coalition is a diverse alliance dedicated to balancing the protection of confidential 
health information with the need for efficient, interoperable systems that enhance healthcare 
delivery. The Coalition’s aim is to safeguard the privacy of healthcare consumers while improving the 
essential flow of information necessary to deliver high-quality, timely, and effective care and 
facilitating the development of innovative medical interventions. 
HLC and the Coalition have long championed technology enablement and moving toward real-time 
prior authorization decisions. This has included advancing interoperability initiatives such as the 
Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) and Fast Healthcare 
 
1 CMS, Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs, 91 Fed. Reg. 19890 (Apr. 14, 2026), 
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-04-14/pdf/2026-07205.pdf. 
 
2 
Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standards, while always emphasizing the need to minimize 
burdens on stakeholders and ensure they have the necessary resources and on ramps for effective 
implementation. 
HLC and its members are committed to collaborating with CMS and serving as a resource in 
advancing these efforts. HLC joined CMS’s Health Tech Ecosystem as a Friend of the Ecosystem2 
and supported the agency’s launch of the health plan pledge3 to improve and streamline prior 
authorization, and this year’s addition of the multi-sector electronic prior authorization pledge4 to the 
Health Tech Ecosystem. Many HLC member companies have also participated in these initiatives, 
demonstrating broad private-sector commitment to improving and accelerating prior authorization 
processes. 
 
HLC and the Coalition strongly support CMS’s goal to modernize prior authorization through 
improved interoperability. We offer targeted recommendations below to ensure the final policies are 
practical, reduce administrative burden, and improve patients’ timely access to care. In addition, we 
provide detailed feedback in response to the proposed rule’s Request for Information (RFI) on 
cybersecurity. 
 
Expedited Decision Timeframes: Advancing Real-Time Prior Authorization  
We support CMS’ goal of accelerating prior authorization decisions for drugs and emphasize that 
timeframes must be applied only to complete requests and implemented in ways that avoid 
unintended increases in denials, appeals, and administrative burden.  
In particular, we appreciate CMS building on the 2024 final rule that applied clinical decision 
timeframes for non-drug items and services, applying timeframes to prior authorizations for drugs. 
We commend the inclusion of a requirement to provide specific reasons for prior authorization 
denials within the required timeframes, so that providers have clear insight into each decision. HLC 
and the Coalition also support the proposed expedited timeframes for drugs (generally 72-hours for 
standard requests and 24-hours for expedited requests, with program-specific variations) and offer 
the below recommendations to ensure the timeframes only apply to complete requests and allow 
sufficient flexibility in workflows.   
Recommendations:  
• 
Adopt a complete request standard, with decision timeframes beginning only once the 
minimum necessary clinical information is submitted. While we are optimistic that 
increased adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) will improve submission completeness over 
time, in the interim CMS should establish a mechanism to ensure that incomplete requests 
do not trigger compressed decision timelines that could lead to avoidable denials, 
resubmissions, appeals, and added administrative burden. CMS should also require prompt, 
 
2 CMS, Friend of the Ecosystem, https://www.cms.gov/health-tech-ecosystem/early-adopters/friend. 
3 HHS, HHS Secretary Kennedy, CMS Administrator Oz Secure Industry Pledge to Fix Broken Prior 
Authorization System (June 23, 2025), https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/kennedy-oz-cms-secure-
healthcare-industry-pledge-to-fix-prior-authorization-system.html. 
4 CMS, Additional Use Case – Electronic Prior Authorization, https://www.cms.gov/health-tech-
ecosystem/early-adopters/epa. 
 
3 
specific notice of any missing elements so that incomplete request determinations do not 
create avoidable delays or administrative burden. 
• 
Provide clarity and flexibility in prior authorization workflows. CMS proposes to require 
the use of distinct standards for drugs covered under the pharmacy benefit and for drugs 
covered under the medical benefit. Drugs covered under the pharmacy benefit would use 
National Council for Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) SCRIPT-based transactions, 
while drugs covered under the medical benefit would use FHIR-based workflows such as 
Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), and 
Prior Authorization Support (PAS). CMS also acknowledges that a single drug may be 
categorized differently across payers based on coverage design. HLC and the Coalition 
encourage CMS to provide additional flexibility in how prior authorization requests are routed 
and processed across these technical pathways. Such flexibility would enable integrated, 
episode-based workflows when drug regimens span both the pharmacy and medical 
benefits, so that providers are not required to navigate separate, duplicative processes. It is 
also important that CMS clearly identify for providers which pathway applies to a given drug 
so that requests can be initiated through the appropriate channel without confusion. 
Reducing Burden and Enhancing Transparency: Centering Patient Care 
As prior authorization processes become more data-driven, transparency and streamlined 
information exchange must be designed to enhance patient care and minimize administrative 
burden. We support CMS’ proposal to extend prior authorization transparency and reporting 
requirements to drugs and share the agency’s goal to advance FHIR-based standards and 
technology enablement to support more efficient, interoperable prior authorization processes. To 
support these goals and minimize unintended burden, we offer the following recommendations. 
Recommendations:  
• 
Streamline reporting requirements. CMS should align and simplify reporting across federal 
and state programs to eliminate duplication and ensure metrics are consistent, meaningful, 
and actionable for patients, providers, and policymakers. For example, CMS should clarify 
how to account for transactions in which CRD and DTR processes determine that no prior 
authorization is required, so that reporting accurately reflects prior authorization volume and 
does not inadvertently encourage unnecessary PAS transactions or create misaligned 
incentives. 
• 
Incentivize technology adoption and upgrades. CMS should provide financial and 
technical support when new technology requirements are introduced, particularly to assist 
providers in rural and underserved areas in meeting interoperability and reporting 
expectations. We encourage CMS to leverage ongoing CMS and industry initiatives, 
including real-time health plan efforts and the Health Tech Ecosystem electronic prior 
authorization initiative, to help target and promote scalable and sustainable adoption. 
• 
Promote use of real-time, patient-specific pharmacy benefit information at the point of 
prescribing. CMS should encourage the use of patient-specific, real-time pharmacy benefit 
information in prescribing workflows to help identify prior authorization requirements and 
clinically appropriate covered alternatives before a prescription is transmitted. Enabling this 
capability within clinical workflows can reduce avoidable prior authorization requests, 
minimize delays at the pharmacy, and support more informed, patient-centered prescribing 
decisions. 
 
4 
Implementation Timelines: Supporting Effective Operationalization 
CMS proposes most new requirements, including electronic prior authorization (ePA) for drugs, API 
updates, and new process requirements, to take effect October 1, 2027, with additional reporting and 
transparency requirements beginning in 2028. Implementing these standards will be complex, and 
insufficient lead time could result in rushed deployments, system instability, and unintended 
disruptions to patient care. 
Given the complexity of interoperability upgrades, workflow redesign, and vendor dependencies, 
adequate time and flexibility are essential to ensure successful, sustainable adoption. To support a 
smooth transition, we recommend the following. 
Recommendations: 
• 
Provide a minimum 24-month implementation period. CMS should allow regulated 
entities at least 24 months from the publication of the final rule and accompanying guidance 
to develop, test, and implement new standards. This timeframe will help ensure careful, 
deliberate rollouts and reduce the risk of operational issues that could affect providers and 
patients. 
• 
Allow version flexibility through the transition period. In order to support orderly 
upgrades and minimize disruption, CMS should permit entities to operate on existing or 
earlier versions of applicable standards while establishing clear versioning guardrails until 
the proposed version 2.2 FHIR implementation guides become mandatory. CMS should 
clarify which versions remain compliant during the transition period. CMS should also 
encourage a minimum level of backward compatibility and error handling, similar to HL7 Da 
Vinci versioning practices, to reduce complexity and support reliable interoperability across 
systems.  
• 
Adopt a phased implementation approach. CMS should prioritize mature, well-tested 
capabilities in early phases while allowing for iterative adoption of more complex functions 
over time, reducing operational risk and enabling continuous improvement. CMS should also 
encourage stakeholder participation in industry-led testing initiatives to validate readiness 
and reduce the risk of deployment disruptions. 
 
Cybersecurity RFI: Ensuring Healthcare System Resilience and Patient Protection 
HLC and the Coalition appreciate CMS’ focus on strengthening healthcare resiliency against cyber 
threats and agree that cybersecurity is fundamentally a patient safety and continuity‑of‑care issue.  
The healthcare sector is uniquely vulnerable to cyberattacks, which can place patient data and care 
delivery at risk and impose significant costs across the system. Nearly all healthcare organizations 
(92%) reported experiencing a cyberattack in 2024.5 These threats originate from a range of actors, 
including sophisticated state‑sponsored entities, organized international criminal networks, and 
malicious insiders. 
 
5 HealthTech Magazine, Cybersecurity in Healthcare: Top Threats to Watch in 2025 (Jan. 2025), 
https://healthtechmagazine.net/article/2025/01/healthcare-cybersecurity-threats-2025-perfcon. 
 
5 
The impacts of cybersecurity breaches in healthcare are significant and multifaceted, affecting 
patient care, systemwide operations, and overall costs. Most critically, cyber incidents can disrupt 
clinical care, delay treatments and procedures, and jeopardize patient safety. At the same time, the 
healthcare system’s increasing interconnectedness means that an attack on one entity can have 
cascading effects across providers, payers, and affiliated organizations, with operational disruptions 
that may last for months. Finally, cyberattacks impose substantial financial burdens. In 2025, the 
average breach cost in healthcare was $7.42 million, the highest among industries for the twelfth 
consecutive year. Although this represents a decrease from 2024 ($9.77 million), healthcare 
breaches remained disproportionately costly, averaging nearly 70 percent higher than the global 
cross-industry average of $4.4 million. 6 
HLC and the Coalition encourage CMS to consider the recommendations outlined in their 2025 
cybersecurity framework, which defines complementary private and public sector roles before, 
during, and after a cyberattack.7 The recommendations below are organized across these core 
categories. 
Prevention Recommendations: Hygiene and Resilience 
• 
Promote law enforcement and information-sharing as international priorities. CMS 
should encourage and support whole-of-government coordination that strengthens cross-
border deterrence, disruption, and accountability for cybercriminals targeting U.S. healthcare. 
• 
Bolster public-private collaboration over cybersecurity prevention measures. CMS 
should advance approaches that recognize and align with established, risk-based 
cybersecurity frameworks, avoiding one-size-fits-all requirements that may not scale across 
diverse entities.  
• 
Enhance public-private information-sharing. CMS should support expanded participation 
and faster, more actionable threat-sharing, leveraging existing sector mechanisms and 
incentives that improve readiness and resilience.  
• 
Use practical, risk-based, outcomes-focused expectations that scale. CMS should 
prioritize measurable risk reduction and allow entities to meet expectations through 
recognized security frameworks and scalable practices, rather than prescriptive, one-size-
fits-all controls that may not fit diverse operating environments. 
• 
Support adoption of AI-driven cybersecurity capabilities and coordination on AI-
related risks. CMS should encourage the use of AI and machine learning to improve 
vulnerability management, threat detection, and response at scale, while supporting 
sustained public-private collaboration to assess emerging AI-enabled threats and promote 
safeguards that reduce malicious misuse. 
• 
Ensure cybersecurity is embedded as data exchange and connectivity expand. CMS 
should ensure that policies advancing interoperable exchange, including application 
programming interfaces (APIs) and network connections, are paired with appropriate 
 
6 IBM, Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025, https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach. 
7 HLC, Confidentiality Coalition, and Manatt, Phelps & Phillips, LLP, Cybersecurity in Healthcare: Defining 
Private and Public Sector Responsibility (July 9, 2025), https://www.hlc.org/report/cybersecurity-in-
healthcare-defining-private-and-public-sector-responsibility/. 
 
6 
safeguards (such as strong authentication, least-privilege access, and monitoring) so 
expanded connectivity does not unintentionally increase exposure. As systems become 
more connected and reliance on third-party vendors and technologies grows, often outside 
the direct control of individual entities, these safeguards are critical to maintaining system 
security and resilience. 
Response Recommendations: Restoring and Reporting 
• 
Harmonize and streamline breach reporting requirements to reduce duplication and 
accelerate action. The current patchwork of inconsistent reporting triggers, timelines, and 
processes can divert resources away from response and restoration. CMS should work with 
relevant federal agencies, including the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) and others, to 
promote alignment and simplification, including reducing duplicative or overlapping reporting 
obligations, to allow organizations to focus on rapid response and continuity of care for 
patients. 
• 
Improve real-time information-sharing during incidents. CMS should coordinate with 
other HHS agencies and federal partners to advance policies that enable rapid exchange of 
actionable threat indicators and defensive measures across healthcare entities, helping 
victims restore operations and reconnect safely. 
• 
Address resilience risks from key intermediaries and “single points of failure.” CMS 
should consider how its policies can support continuity planning and rapid transition 
capabilities when clearinghouses or other critical service providers are impacted, minimizing 
downstream disruptions to care and payment operations. 
• 
Support continuity of payments and financial stability during major cyber events. 
Given the operational and patient-care impacts associated with system downtime, CMS 
should consider mechanisms within its authority to help stabilize providers during significant 
cybersecurity disruptions, enabling them to sustain care delivery while restoring systems. 
Recovery Recommendations: Rebuilding and Learning  
• 
Streamline recovery approvals and relief processes. CMS should simplify and coordinate 
post-incident relief pathways, particularly for quality reporting and other program obligations, 
to enable organizations to prioritize restoring safe clinical operations and essential systems. 
• 
Mitigate liability and reward responsible action. CMS should work with other federal 
agencies to support incentives and policy approaches that recognize robust cybersecurity 
programs and responsible incident handling, helping to align accountability with practical 
realities and encouraging ongoing investment in resilience. 
• 
Incentivize and support cybersecurity improvements. CMS should work with relevant 
federal partners and programs to promote financial and technical assistance, approaches 
that help providers, particularly small, rural, and underserved organizations, strengthen 
controls, improve resilience, and access cybersecurity expertise. 
• 
Support cybersecurity workforce capacity. CMS should work with relevant federal 
partners and stakeholders to support workforce development, training, and recruitment 
efforts, particularly for small, rural, and underserved providers that face significant challenges 
in hiring and retaining cybersecurity professionals, which can limit their ability to effectively 
prevent, detect, and respond to cyber threats. We appreciate the Administration’s 
 
7 
emphasizing support for critical infrastructure, including rural providers, in the recent 
Executive Order on promoting AI innovation and cybersecurity capacity.8 Such support could 
be modeled after services already offered by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) 
and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to state, local, tribal, and 
territorial governments. For example, in 2024, DHS offered 839 grants to these governments 
to develop cybersecurity policies, hire cybersecurity contractors, upgrade equipment, and 
implement multifactor authentication.9  
• 
Embed “lessons learned” to strengthen future preparedness. CMS should work with 
other federal agencies and stakeholders to encourage practices that incorporate post-
incident learnings into ongoing security planning, fostering continuous improvement and 
reducing recurrence of similar failures. 
 
Conclusion 
HLC and the Coalition’s cross-sector membership brings deep expertise in interoperability, prior 
authorization, and cybersecurity resilience across the healthcare ecosystem. We encourage CMS to 
draw on this expertise in refining the policies proposed in this rule and in advancing practical, 
coordinated approaches that strengthen patient care, reduce administrative burden, and support a 
more resilient healthcare system. 
Thank you for your continued leadership streamlining prior authorization and improving 
interoperability. If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me at abanks@hlc.org. 
Sincerely,  
 
 
 
 
Angela Banks,  
Head of Policy and Advocacy 
 
8 Exec. Order No. 14,409, Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security (June 2, 
2026), https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/06/promoting-advanced-artificial-
intelligence-innovation-and-security/. 
9 GAO, Cybersecurity: DHS Implemented a Grant Program to Enable State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial 
Governments to Improve Security, GAO-25-107313 (Apr. 29, 2025), https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-
25-107313.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Healthcare Leadership Council (HLC) and the Confidentiality Coalition
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Healthcare industry coalition / Privacy and confidentiality coalition
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** HLC represents CEOs and C-suite executives from hospitals, academic health centers, health plans, pharmaceutical and device companies, laboratories, distributors, post-acute care, homecare, GPOs, and health IT companies. The Confidentiality Coalition focuses on balancing health information privacy with interoperable data exchange.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

HLC and the Coalition strongly support CMS's goal to modernize prior authorization through interoperability, while recommending operational refinements to avoid new burden. They ask CMS to apply timeframes only to complete requests, allow workflow flexibility between NCPDP and FHIR pathways, streamline reporting, incentivize technology adoption, provide at least 24 months for implementation, allow version flexibility and phased adoption, and strengthen cybersecurity resilience through risk-based public-private approaches.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL/RFI.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** References CMS-0062-P and the 2024 final rule; no specific CFR sections central to the comment.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR; Da Vinci CRD, DTR, PAS; NCPDP SCRIPT-based transactions; pharmacy benefit real-time information; APIs; version 2.2 FHIR implementation guides; TEFCA; AI-enabled cybersecurity; authentication, least privilege, monitoring.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Expedited decision timeframes and complete requests**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** HLC supports accelerated timeframes and specific denial reasons but warns that incomplete requests could trigger avoidable denials, resubmissions, appeals, and burden.
- **Specific request:** Apply timeframes only to complete requests; require prompt, specific notice of missing elements; avoid triggering compressed timelines before minimum necessary information is submitted.

**Topic 2: Medical vs pharmacy benefit workflow flexibility**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** CMS proposes different standards for pharmacy benefit drugs (NCPDP SCRIPT) and medical benefit drugs (FHIR CRD/DTR/PAS), but drugs may be categorized differently across payers and regimens may span benefits.
- **Specific request:** Provide routing and processing flexibility across technical pathways, allow integrated episode-based workflows, and clearly identify which pathway applies for a given drug.

**Topic 3: Reporting and transparency**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** HLC supports transparency but warns duplicative or poorly designed reporting could be burdensome or misaligned.
- **Specific request:** Align and simplify reporting across federal and state programs; clarify how CRD/DTR determinations that no PA is required should be reported.

**Topic 4: Technology adoption and real-time benefit information**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Technology requirements will not reduce burden unless providers and stakeholders can adopt them, including rural and underserved providers.
- **Specific request:** Provide financial/technical support for adoption; leverage CMS/industry Health Tech Ecosystem efforts; promote real-time, patient-specific pharmacy benefit information at prescribing.

**Topic 5: Implementation timeline and version flexibility**
- **Provision ID:** IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Implementation of ePA, API updates, reporting, workflow redesign, and vendor dependencies is complex; rushed deployments could cause instability.
- **Specific request:** Provide at least 24 months after final rule and guidance; allow earlier/existing standard versions during transition with guardrails; adopt phased implementation prioritizing mature capabilities.

**Topic 6: Cybersecurity RFI**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI; PRIVACY-SECURITY
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Expanded connectivity increases cyber risk; cybersecurity is a patient safety and continuity-of-care issue.
- **Specific request:** Use risk-based, outcomes-focused expectations; support public-private collaboration, threat sharing, AI-driven security capabilities, harmonized breach reporting, continuity of payments, recovery relief, workforce support, and rural/underserved cybersecurity assistance.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12/S15/S21/S28:** HLC addresses medical/pharmacy drug PA workflows, benefit categorization, and the need for flexible routing across NCPDP and FHIR pathways.
- **S16/S20:** HLC supports specific denial reasons and expedited timeframes but asks CMS to apply timeframes only to complete requests.
- **S23/S24/S29/S30/S34/S35:** HLC comments on reporting design, API-related metrics, privacy protections, and how to avoid duplicative or misleading reporting.
- **S37:** HLC highlights implementation challenges, provider adoption needs, and the importance of financial/technical support.
- **S47/S50/S53/S54:** HLC addresses implementation timing, standards maturity/version flexibility, phased implementation, and testing.
- **S60-S65:** HLC asks for version flexibility and guardrails until proposed FHIR IG version 2.2 becomes mandatory.
- **S66-S82:** HLC responds to the cybersecurity/resiliency RFI with prevention, response, and recovery recommendations.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Adopt a complete-request standard for prior authorization timeframes.
2. Require prompt, specific notice of missing elements in incomplete requests.
3. Provide flexibility in routing PA requests between NCPDP pharmacy-benefit and FHIR medical-benefit pathways.
4. Clearly identify the applicable pathway for a given drug.
5. Streamline reporting across programs and ensure metrics are meaningful.
6. Clarify reporting treatment for CRD/DTR outcomes where no PA is required.
7. Provide financial and technical support for technology adoption, especially rural and underserved providers.
8. Promote patient-specific real-time pharmacy benefit information at prescribing.
9. Provide at least a 24-month implementation period after final rule and guidance.
10. Allow version flexibility during transition and clarify compliant versions.
11. Adopt phased implementation focused first on mature, tested capabilities.
12. Strengthen cybersecurity prevention, incident response, recovery, workforce, and public-private information sharing.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Incomplete requests under compressed timeframes, duplicative workflows across medical/pharmacy benefits, reporting burden, insufficient implementation time, uneven technology adoption, and cybersecurity risks from expanded connectivity.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Avoidable denials and appeals, administrative burden, workflow fragmentation, patient care disruptions, cyber incidents affecting care delivery and costs.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Vendor dependencies, provider technology gaps, rural/underserved resource constraints, version transitions, benefit categorization differences, third-party cybersecurity risk.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** HLC cites cybersecurity data: 92% of healthcare organizations reported a cyberattack in 2024; average healthcare breach cost in 2025 was $7.42 million; healthcare breaches remained nearly 70% higher than the global cross-industry average of $4.4 million.
- **Studies or research referenced:** HealthTech Magazine cybersecurity threat reporting; IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025; HLC/Confidentiality Coalition/Manatt 2025 cybersecurity framework; GAO cybersecurity grants information.
- **Examples provided:** Incomplete PA submissions leading to avoidable denials; integrated regimens spanning medical and pharmacy benefits; clearinghouses or critical intermediaries as single points of failure during cyber incidents.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Health plans, providers, patients, pharmacies, rural/underserved providers, health IT vendors, clearinghouses, cybersecurity teams, federal agencies.
- **Economic implications:** Technology mandates and cyber incidents can create significant cost; support and phased implementation can reduce burden and instability.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible with 24-month runway, version flexibility, testing, phased adoption, and practical cybersecurity safeguards.
- **Patient care impact:** Properly implemented interoperability can reduce delays; poor implementation or cyber disruptions could harm continuity and access.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with substantial operational refinements
- **Tone:** Professional, technical, collaborative, risk-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "HLC and the Coalition strongly support CMS’s goal to modernize prior authorization through improved interoperability." - Context: Overall position.
2. "timeframes must be applied only to complete requests" - Context: Expedited decision timeframe recommendation.
3. "CMS should allow regulated entities at least 24 months from the publication of the final rule and accompanying guidance" - Context: Implementation timeline request.
4. "cybersecurity is fundamentally a patient safety and continuity-of-care issue" - Context: Cybersecurity RFI response.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Requests at least 24 months, phased implementation, and version transition guardrails.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Discusses financial/technical support, breach costs, and resource needs.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Focuses on avoiding incomplete-request denials, duplicative workflows, and reporting burden.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Major cybersecurity and privacy/resilience RFI section.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Calls out support for rural and underserved providers.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Extensive discussion of standards, routing, versions, testing, and cybersecurity feasibility.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Requests version flexibility until FHIR IG v2.2 and mature capabilities are ready.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Seeks to prevent delays, denials, and cyber disruptions that affect care.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Not a primary topic.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Public-private collaboration, threat sharing, CMS/industry initiatives.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Central discussion of NCPDP vs FHIR pathways.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports meaningful reporting and missing-information notices.
- [ ] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not central, though scalable expectations are discussed.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Addresses workflows across prescribing, routing, reporting, and incident response.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Discusses vendors, intermediaries, clearinghouses, and technology dependencies.
